To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the use of bioassays is essential to monitor environmental levels of EASs, and (2) the use of chemical methods for monitoring environmental levels of EDSs is essential to monitor the effects of exposure to EASs.

(1) a combination of chemical and bioassays is the best way to monitor environmental exposures to endocrine active substances, (2) a combination of different types of bioassays, including in vitro and in vivo assays, is the best way for monitoring environmental exposures to EASs, (3) the use of in vitro bioassay data for exposure assessment is complicated, (4) a combination of in vitro and in silico data is the best way of estimating the in vivo potency

the analytical methods are well developed and validated for many EASs, but that the analytical methods for many EAS classes are not sufficiently sensitive to measure the levels of exposure in the environment and that the bioanalytical methods are not sufficiently specific to measure the levels in environmental samples.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of EASs in food and the aquatic environment.
the development of methods for monitoring EASs in food and the aquatic environment.
the development of methods of analysis for the determination of residues of endocrinedisrupting chemicals in food and the determination of the endocrine activity of these chemicals.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the analytical techniques are adequate to support the monitoring of residues of EASs in food and the aquatic environment.
there is a need to develop and validate more sensitive and selective methods to measure residues of EASs in environmental matrices and in foods.
there is a lack of data on EASs in foods and the environment and that the data are not sufficient to assess the risk to human health.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the current state-of-the-art for chemical analysis of EASs is adequate for monitoring of environmental levels, and that the bioanalytical methods are complementary and can be used to provide a more complete picture of exposure.
there is a need for more sensitive, selective, and specific chemical methods for EASs, especially for the low molecular weight substances.

we have made good progress in the development of analytical techniques for EASs, but that there is still much to do in order to develop a full suite of analytical techniques for the wide range of EASs of interest to the scientific and regulatory communities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the current analytical methods and techniques are sufficient for the analysis of most EASs in the environment.
a number of analytical methods are now available for the determination of a wide range of EASs in environmental and food samples.
a combination of chemical and bioassays are needed for monitoring of the most important classes of EAS.
